title: Preventive Health Screenings: What Adults Need and When
content:
Preventive screenings detect disease early — often before symptoms appear — when it is most treatable. The following are key screenings recommended for adults by the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF), a federally appointed independent panel.

Blood pressure: Screened at every routine health visit. High blood pressure (hypertension) — defined as 130/80 mmHg or above — often has no symptoms but greatly increases risk of heart attack and stroke. Normal blood pressure is below 120/80 mmHg.

Cholesterol (lipid panel): Adults 35+ (men) and 45+ (women) who are at increased cardiovascular risk; earlier screening for adults with risk factors such as diabetes, smoking, obesity, or family history of early heart disease.

Blood glucose / type 2 diabetes: Adults aged 35–70 who are overweight or obese. Testing may start earlier for those with additional risk factors.

Colorectal cancer screening: Adults aged 45–75. Options include a stool-based test annually (high-sensitivity guaiac FOBT or FIT test) or a colonoscopy every 10 years. Discussion with a provider helps choose the appropriate method.

Breast cancer (mammography): Women aged 40–74; the USPSTF recommends biennial (every 2 years) screening for women 50–74, and shared decision-making for women 40–49 based on individual risk and preference.

Cervical cancer (Pap smear / HPV co-test): Women aged 21–65. Pap smear every 3 years for women 21–29; Pap smear plus HPV test every 5 years (or Pap alone every 3 years) for women 30–65.

Lung cancer (low-dose CT scan): Adults aged 50–80 with a 20 pack-year smoking history who currently smoke or quit within the past 15 years.

Abdominal aortic aneurysm (ultrasound): Men aged 65–75 who have ever smoked.

Skin self-examination: Monthly self-checks for new or changing moles, spots, or lesions. Report any ABCDE signs — Asymmetry, irregular Border, multiple Colours, Diameter larger than a pencil eraser, or Evolution (change over time) — to a healthcare provider.

This list reflects major USPSTF recommendations. Individual needs vary based on personal and family medical history; your primary care provider is the best resource for a personalised screening schedule.
source: Original — based on U.S. Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) recommendations (public domain, federal government publication)
